value.overview: The Sooty Thrush (Turdus nigrescens) is a large, dark thrush restricted to the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is especially associated with cool, wet mountain landscapes and often feeds in open ground, scrub, forest edges, and high-elevation pasture. Its nearly black plumage contrasts strongly with its orange bill, eye-ring, legs, and feet. In Costa Rica, it is a characteristic resident of the country's volcanic and Talamancan highlands.
value.classification: The Sooty Thrush belongs to the thrush family, Turdidae, and the genus Turdus. It is generally treated as a monotypic species.
value.identification: Adults are large thrushes with mostly sooty black or brownish-black plumage. The lores, wings, and tail are especially dark, while the pale eye contrasts with a bright orange bill, orange bare eye-ring, and orange legs. Females are generally browner and paler than males and may show faint darker streaking on the throat. Juveniles are browner, with buff streaks above and spotted, buff-toned underparts. The Mountain Thrush is browner overall and has darker bare parts.
value.rangeHabitat: The Sooty Thrush has a localized range in the mountains of Costa Rica and extends into far western Panama, mainly in Chiriquí. In Costa Rica it occurs in the Cordillera Volcánica Central and Cordillera de Talamanca, usually from about 2,150 meters upward and most commonly above 2,400 meters. It uses edges of montane evergreen forest, humid and semi-humid montane scrub, páramo, boggy areas, second growth, and high-elevation pastures. It may also visit open areas near forest.
value.migrationStatus: It is primarily a year-round resident in Costa Rica. Some individuals move to somewhat lower elevations after breeding, so local seasonal changes in abundance can occur, but it is not a long-distance migrant.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly from March through May. The species builds a bulky cup nest from twigs, rootlets, lichens, mosses, and fine grasses, sometimes with mud. Nests are typically placed in a tall shrub or tree roughly 2–8 meters above the ground. The usual clutch is two greenish-blue eggs. Details of incubation, nestling development, and parental care remain incompletely documented.
value.dietFeeding: The Sooty Thrush eats insects, spiders, and other small invertebrates, together with fruits and berries. It commonly forages on the ground in open sites and along forest edges, probing grass clumps and turning over leaves with its bill. Fruit availability can be important outside the breeding period. Birds may forage alone, in pairs, or in small, loose groups.
value.behavior: This thrush is often active and conspicuous in open highland habitats, although fog, dense vegetation, and dark plumage can make it difficult to see. It spends substantial time walking or hopping on the ground while searching for food. Its song consists of short phrases repeated several times, with pauses between phrases. Calls include low, grating notes and thinner rolling or harsh sounds.

conservation.populationTrend: A reliable current global population trend is not clearly documented.
